title: The End of "Good Enough" Timing Analysis - Semiwiki
gist: Vendor-authored analysis (promoting ClockEdge) argues that at 5nm and below, static timing analysis alone no longer captures a clock network's real electrical behavior—jitter, power, duty cycle, aging, and supply-noise interactions compound as margins shrink—and that distributed SPICE-accurate simulation is now becoming practical at full SoC scale, enabling engineers to optimize (not just verify) clock networks, which matters most for power/frequency-constrained AI-workload chips.

themes.theme: Why static timing analysis alone is reaching its limits

insights.claim: At older process nodes there was enough design margin to treat timing, power, jitter, and other electrical effects as separate, independently manageable analyses; at 5nm, 3nm, 2nm and below, that margin cushion has shrunk to the point where a few picoseconds can materially affect design outcomes.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Frames a structural inflection point in verification methodology tied directly to node scaling—relevant for EDA vendors and chip design teams assessing when new signoff methodologies (beyond legacy STA) become commercially necessary rather than optional.
insights.quote: At 5nm, 3nm, 2nm and below, that cushion is getting smaller. Supply voltages are lower, interconnect effects are larger, power delivery has become more challenging, and a few picoseconds can materially affect design outcomes.

insights.claim: A clock network can pass timing closure while leaving important questions unanswered about how much margin is physically required, how much jitter accumulates end-to-end, how supply noise affects clock behavior, whether clock power is higher than necessary, and how aging will affect the clock over the product's lifetime.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Provides an explicit checklist investors/engineers can use to evaluate whether a design team's current signoff methodology is actually sufficient for advanced nodes versus merely 'checking the box' on timing closure.
insights.quote: A clock network can meet its timing requirements and still leave important engineering questions such as these unanswered.
insights.locator: timing closure and clock understanding section

insights.claim: Because separate analysis methodologies (STA, power integrity, jitter, aging, variation) each make independent assumptions about effects handled elsewhere, they cannot capture how those effects interact electrically across a complete clock network—a limitation that matters increasingly as design margins tighten.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Explains the specific mechanistic gap (siloed assumptions across separate tools) that creates the market opportunity for integrated, full-network electrical analysis tools like ClockEdge's—a thesis for why point-tool EDA methodology may be losing ground to integrated electrical-analysis platforms at advanced nodes.
insights.quote: When a physical system is decomposed into separate analyses, each methodology must make assumptions about the effects being handled elsewhere.

insights.claim: Design changes intended to improve one clock-network metric can degrade another: upsizing a clock cell may improve slew but increase power and local supply disturbance, while downsizing may reduce power but change delay, jitter sensitivity, and duty-cycle behavior.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Illustrates a concrete engineering trade-off dynamic that makes siloed, single-metric optimization risky at advanced nodes—supports the case for holistic, cross-metric electrical analysis tools over point solutions.
insights.quote: Upsizing a clock cell may improve slew, but it can also increase power and local supply disturbance. Downsizing may reduce power while changing delay, jitter sensitivity, and duty-cycle behavior.

themes.theme: Margin is not free, and more margin is not more understanding

insights.claim: Extra clock margin added to compensate for analysis uncertainty is not free—it can translate into lower frequency, higher operating voltage, increased power, larger cells, more buffering, reduced thermal headroom, or reduced design flexibility elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Quantifies the real opportunity cost of conservative margining practices—relevant for chip design teams and AI-accelerator makers under intense power/frequency pressure, where excess margin directly erodes competitive performance-per-watt.
insights.quote: Additional clock margin can translate into lower frequency, higher operating voltage, increased power, larger cells, more buffering, reduced thermal headroom, or less flexibility elsewhere in the design.
insights.locator: more margin is not more understanding section

insights.claim: The key engineering question is not whether margin should exist, but how much of that margin is required by the clock's actual electrical behavior versus how much is simply protecting against what the analysis methodology cannot directly see.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for evaluating margin decisions in any advanced-node chip design—useful heuristic for assessing whether a design team is over-engineering (and thus sacrificing performance) due to methodology blind spots rather than genuine physical necessity.
insights.quote: The more useful question is: How much of that margin is required by the electrical behavior of the clock, and how much is protecting against what the methodology cannot directly see?
insights.locator: more margin is not more understanding section

insights.claim: A few picoseconds of unnecessary clock margin or a small amount of excess clock power appear insignificant in isolation but scale across large designs and persist for every operating cycle, making the cost meaningful in high-performance AI-workload chips where power and frequency are under intense pressure.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Directly ties clock-margin optimization to AI-accelerator competitiveness, where compounding small inefficiencies across billions of cycles and huge core counts can materially affect a chip's power/performance envelope versus rivals.
insights.quote: This is particularly important in high-performance designs such as those powering AI workloads, where both power and frequency are under intense pressure.
insights.locator: timing is closed but is the clock optimized section

themes.theme: The technology shift: SPICE-accurate analysis becoming practical at SoC scale

insights.claim: Historically, obtaining full electrical visibility into a clock network required SPICE-level transistor accuracy, which came with prohibitive capacity and runtime penalties, forcing design teams to trade off detailed accuracy against large-scale analysis capacity.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Establishes the historical technical barrier that new distributed-computing approaches are now overcoming—key context for why full-network SPICE-accurate analysis at SoC scale is presented as a genuinely new capability rather than an incremental improvement.
insights.quote: Historically, however, there has been a practical barrier to obtaining that level of visibility across an entire SoC clock network: SPICE accuracy came with a capacity and runtime penalty.

insights.claim: Distributed computing and simulation advances are making SPICE-accurate electrical analysis practical for complete clock networks at full SoC scale within usable engineering runtimes, a tradeoff that is described as 'beginning to change.'
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Central commercial claim of the piece: a previously infeasible engineering capability (full-chip SPICE-accurate clock analysis) is now becoming commercially viable, which is the market opportunity ClockEdge (and by extension any competing full-network electrical-analysis EDA vendor) is targeting.
insights.quote: Distributed computing and advances in simulation are making SPICE-accurate electrical analysis practical for complete clock networks at SoC scale and within usable engineering runtimes.
insights.locator: that tradeoff is beginning to change section

insights.claim: Full-network electrical insight can be introduced early, around clock tree synthesis when implementation choices can still be changed, and then carried through sign-off and into silicon correlation—rather than being applied only at the end of the design flow.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Implies a shift-left opportunity in the design flow: earlier electrical visibility could reduce costly late-stage design changes, a potential productivity and schedule-risk-reduction benefit for chip design teams adopting this class of tool.
insights.quote: Electrical insight can be introduced around clock tree synthesis, when implementation choices can still be changed, and carried through sign-off and into silicon correlation.
insights.locator: and once that level of analysis paragraph

insights.claim: ClockEdge is positioned as the company addressing this gap, providing scalable SPICE-accurate analysis of complete clock networks—from PLL/clock source to sequential endpoints—across timing, power, jitter, duty cycle, aging, sensitivity, and optimization via a distributed architecture.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Names the specific commercial vendor and product category this sponsored analysis is promoting—useful for tracking ClockEdge as an emerging EDA point-solution vendor in the advanced-node clock-analysis niche, alongside incumbents like Cadence, Synopsys, and Ansys.
insights.quote: ClockEdge® is a company that addresses the needs discussed here. It provides scalable, SPICE-accurate analysis of complete clock networks, from the PLL or clock source to sequential endpoints, across timing, power, jitter, duty cycle, aging, sensitivity, and optimization.

insights.claim: The article explicitly frames its argument not as replacing static timing analysis but as complementing it—STA remains fundamental for capacity, coverage, and efficiency, while the new electrical-analysis layer addresses what STA alone cannot reveal about a clock network's true behavior.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Positions the emerging full-network electrical analysis category as additive rather than disruptive/replacement technology for incumbent STA tools—implies incumbents (Cadence, Synopsys) could integrate or partner rather than being displaced, a relevant competitive-dynamics read for EDA sector investors.
insights.quote: STA will remain fundamental to semiconductor design because nothing else provides its extraordinary combination of capacity, coverage, and efficiency. What may be reaching its limit is the assumption that timing closure alone is a sufficient proxy for understanding the electrical behavior of the clock network.
